items.note: Mixed forests on Vindhyans in the district: dry exposed sites, teak 40-60 per cent, grass and shrub ground-cover.
Mixed forests on Vindhyan sandstones and resultant soils (Shamshabad, Gyaraspur ranges): no teak, shallow sandy loam.
Khair-dominated dry mixed deciduous forest on lateritic soil in Sironj range.
Dendrocalamus strictus the only bamboo in the District, along the Dudhia river.
Grass reserves, medicinal plants, gums and mahua in the District's forests.
Decline of wild life in the District through cultivation, forest destruction and poaching; later game protection.
List of mammals found in the District.
Table of wild animals reported in 1968 by shooting block; includes an 'Udaipura' block in Gyaraspur Range.
Birds of the District, including migratory water fowl in winter.
Fish fauna of Vidisha District and aquatic species.
Dry climate, pleasant nights praised by the Mughals as Shab-i-Malwa.
Monsoon onset in June; division of the year into four seasons.
Average annual rainfall 1,229.9 mm; 92 per cent in monsoon months.
Extremes of annual rainfall 1901-1950 (149 per cent in 1948; 50 per cent in 1905).
Low-rainfall years at Vidisha and Basoda.
Rainy days at Basoda to Mohammadgarh; heaviest 24-hour rainfall 360.2 mm at Basoda, 1951.
Seasonal temperatures: May hottest (about 40C mean maximum), January coldest, cold waves.
Humidity and sky conditions in the District.
Monsoon depressions, thunderstorms and duststorms.
Palaeolithic tools in the Betwa, Bina, Dhasan and Keothan valleys.
Chalcolithic tools and painted wares (1000-700 B.C.) and microlithic blades in an ancient mound of the District.
Puranic and Skanda Purana references to Vidisha as janapada and tirtha; Anguttara Nikaya places it in Avanti Janapada.
Region known as Dasharna with Vidisha or Besnagar as capital; variant names of Vidisha.
Vidisha's prosperity from cross-roads of two trade routes, including a branch through the Betwa valley.
Sanchi Stupa built largely by donations of Vidisha's business community.
Vidisha as Akara; Sanchi and the Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar.
Asoka's marriage to Devi of Vidisha or Besnagar; Mahendra and Sanghamitra.
Monastery near Sanchi Stupa; fire in Vidisha attributed by some to Chandragupta Maurya.
Copper coins reading Vedisa suggest Vidisha as a temporary independent city state; dated 3rd-2nd century B.C.
Sungas ruled originally as Mauryan feudatories at Vidisha; Pushyamitra and Agnimitra.
Under the Sungas Vidisha became capital of Akara or eastern Malwa.
Asvamedha sacrifice probably performed at Vidisha; Pushyamitra's reign 187-151 B.C.
Heliodorus Garuda pillar at Besnagar erected in fourteenth year of Bhagabhadra.
Earliest archaeological evidence of Vaishnava culture at Vidisha; inscription of King Bhagvata's twelfth year.
Punch marked coins found in the region, use at Vidisha by 4th century B.C.
Vidisha as north-eastern part of the Satavahana empire, changing allegiance.
Inscriptions and coins of Western Kshatrapa houses unearthed in Vidisha.
Coins of Pulumayi and Kshatrapa rulers found in Vidisha show prolonged occupation.
Naga rulers at Vidisha; house probably originated there.
Naga copper coins from excavations at Besnagar.
Vindhyasakti of the Vakatakas mentioned in the puranas as ruler of Vidisha.
Samudragupta's defeat of Naga rulers; tribes near Vidisha.
Two Chandragupta II epigraphs at the Udayagiri caves of Vidisha (Gupta Era 82).
Kalidasa's Meghaduta on Vidisha and its environs.
Early Kalachuris became rulers of Vidisha; Krishnaraja, Sankaragana, Buddharaja.
Buddharaja's Vadner grant of 608 issued from Vaidisa.
Old Besnagar devastated; population moved to east bank, founding Bhilsa.
Bhilsa from Bhailasvamin, sun-god idol temple; inscription under Krishna III.
Vidisha incorporated in the Chandella empire under Dhanga.
Paramara Siyaka II ousts Chandellas; kingdom bounded by Vidisha on the east; Munja.
Bhoja's accession c. 1000, inscriptions 1020-1047, kingdom including Vidisha.
Udayaditya (Bhoja's cousin or brother) reigned to 1086; built the Nilkanthsavar temple at Udaypur, eastern boundary at Vidisha.
Later Paramara fortunes: Naravarman, Yasovarman defeated by Jayasimha Siddharaja.
Chandella Madan Varman's grant in Sudali Visaya (Vidisha) proves reoccupation of the region.
Iltutmish attacked and sacked Bhilsa in 1234, destroying the Vijay Mandir.
Ala-ud-din captured Bhilsa under last Paramara Mahlak Deva.
Malwa Sultanate founded c. 1401 by Dilawar Khan Ghuri.
Rana Sanga bestows territory including Bhilsa on Medini Rai (1518), passed to Salhadi.
Babur's Memoirs record Bhilsa held by Salhadi in 1527.
